candidate.title: Native plugin libraries are dlopen'd with no signature/hash/publisher verification
candidate.root_cause: Plugin::new (plugins.rs:179-203) calls Library::open(path) (dlopen) on any file whose name matches 'plugin_*'+platform DYLIB_SUFFIX under the plugins directory (load_plugin_dir, plugins.rs:301-330), with no code-signing, checksum, or allow-list check of any kind. load_plugin_path (plugins.rs:355-404) explicitly documents this gap: '// to-do validate plugin' / '// to-do check the plugin id (make sure it does not use another plugin's id)' (lines 361-362) — the checks are acknowledged as never implemented.
candidate.entry_point: Any file named plugin_<name><DYLIB_SUFFIX> placed under <share-dir>/RustDesk/plugins/<id>/, reachable via the Zip Slip / absolute-id install bugs above, via any local file-write primitive (e.g. the file-transfer feature, out of this slice), or simply by a user manually copying a downloaded plugin file into that folder — the whole design intends third-party plugins to be sideloaded this way.
candidate.sink: Library::open(path) in Plugin::new, plugins.rs:180-184, followed by unsafe { lib.symbol::<$tp>(...) } lookups (plugins.rs:187-195) that immediately obtain and later invoke the library's init/desc/call/call_with_out_data function pointers with full host-process privileges.
candidate.attack: Attacker gets any correctly-named plugin_*<suffix> file into the plugins directory by any of the above means; on the next load_plugins() (process startup) or plugins::load_plugin(id) call (triggered right after any install, e.g. install::install_plugin_with_url's IPC 'Finished' handler in manager.rs:371), RustDesk dlopen()s and executes the attacker's native code inside the RustDesk process with no verification whatsoever that it is the plugin the user intended, or signed by anyone trusted.
candidate.preconditions: plugin_framework feature enabled (shipped in official desktop builds); attacker needs a file to land in the plugins directory — trivially satisfied by the two path-traversal/write bugs above, or by ordinary plugin sideloading (an explicitly supported flow) from an untrusted plugin author.
candidate.confidence_reason: The lack of any signature/hash check is unambiguous, and confirmed by the code's own '// to-do validate plugin' comment; this is the enabling primitive that turns every write-primitive in this slice into full native code execution.
candidate.disposition_hint: root-cause finding — cite alongside the Zip Slip / absolute-id findings as the reason a mere file-write becomes RCE

verdict.reason:
The code-level defect is confirmed accurate as cited: Plugin::new (plugins.rs:179-203) calls Library::open(path) (dlopen) at line 180 on any file matching plugin_*+DYLIB_SUFFIX found by load_plugin_dir (plugins.rs:301-330), and load_plugin_path (plugins.rs:355-404) contains the exact '// to-do validate plugin' / '// to-do check the plugin id' comments at lines 361-362 with no signature/hash/allow-list check anywhere in the load path. I also checked the one candidate mitigation that exists in this file tree — the 'signature_verification' mechanism (callback_msg.rs request_plugin_sign, plugins.rs METHOD_HANDLE_SIGNATURE_VERIFICATION) — and confirmed it does NOT gate loading: it is a callback the plugin's own native code voluntarily issues AFTER Plugin::new/dlopen and AFTER plugin.init() have already executed with full host privilege (load_plugin_path calls Plugin::new then plugin.init() unconditionally before any signature concept exists), so it cannot prevent the initial code execution this finding describes. The reachability chain to the sink (install::install_plugin_with_url -> InstallStatus::Finished -> manager.rs:371 super::plugins::load_plugin(&id) -> load_plugin_dir -> load_plugin_path -> Plugin::new -> Library::open) is also verified accurate.

However, the stated precondition 'plugin_framework feature enabled (shipped in official desktop builds)' is not supported by this repository's own build tooling and is actually contradicted by it. Cargo.toml:33 defines plugin_framework as an empty, opt-in feature (not in `default = [\"use_dasp\"]`, Cargo.toml:29). build.py's get_features() (build.py:275-289), which is the single source of truth for the release build's `--features` list, only ever appends inline/hwcodec/vram/flutter/unix-file-copy-paste/screencapturekit — plugin_framework is never referenced. Every `cargo build --features ...` invocation in .github/workflows/flutter-build.yml (the official release CI) I found (lines 461, 617, 1589, 1741, 1751, 1919) likewise never includes plugin_framework. A repo-wide grep for the string 'plugin_framework' outside .rs source and Cargo.toml turns up nothing (no README, CI, or Dockerfile reference). So on the evidence available in this snapshot, the entire plugin subsystem — including this unsigned-dlopen sink — is compiled out of the official desktop client and cannot be reached by attacking a stock RustDesk build; it would only apply to a self-compiled or downstream (e.g. Pro/fork) build that explicitly turns the feature on.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same underlying flaw as claimed (Library::open/dlopen with zero signature/hash verification, explicitly marked '// to-do validate plugin'), but gated behind the plugin_framework Cargo feature, which build.py's get_features() and every cargo build --features invocation in .github/workflows/flutter-build.yml omit — the plugin loader (and thus this sink) is not present in official desktop release binaries built from this repo's own tooling. Real bug in the source tree, not evidenced as attacker-reachable in shipped software.
verdict.live_test: Run `strings` (or `nm`/objdump symbol dump) over an official released rustdesk binary/installer (Windows .exe, macOS .dmg contents, or Linux .deb from https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/releases) and grep for 'plugin_' function names (load_plugin_dir, handle_signature_verification, PLUGIN_INFO) or the literal path fragment 'RustDesk/plugins'. Absence confirms the feature is compiled out of shipped builds (matching the static evidence found); presence would restore the original High/Critical rating.
verdict.observed_mitigation: plugin_framework Cargo feature is opt-in and absent from every documented official build path: Cargo.toml default feature list (Cargo.toml:29) excludes it, build.py get_features() (build.py:275-289) never appends it, and no `cargo build --features` string in .github/workflows/flutter-build.yml includes it.

candidate.title: Plugin's self-declared id used unchecked as identity key and (elsewhere) as a filesystem path component — spoofing/collision, no format or uniqueness validation
candidate.root_cause: load_plugin_path takes `id = desc.meta().id.clone()` — a value returned entirely by the loaded native plugin's own desc() FFI callback (see native.rs / mod.rs Desc::from_cstr) — and inserts it unchecked as the key into both PLUGIN_INFO and PLUGINS (plugins.rs:370, 400), with no validation of character class, length, or uniqueness against already-installed plugins. The code's own comments flag this: '// to-do validate plugin' and '// to-do check the plugin id (make sure it does not use another plugin's id)' (plugins.rs:361-362).
candidate.entry_point: desc() FFI export of any loaded native plugin (already covered by the unsigned-dlopen finding above).
candidate.sink: PLUGIN_INFO.write().unwrap().insert(id.clone(), plugin_info) and PLUGINS.write().unwrap().insert(id.clone(), plugin) (plugins.rs:370, 400); every later id-keyed operation (unload_plugin, mark_uninstalled, reload_plugin, handle_ui_event/handle_server_event/handle_client_event dispatch, and get_plugin_dir(id) used for filesystem paths in manager.rs) trusts this same unchecked id.
candidate.attack: A malicious plugin declares desc().meta.id identical to an already-installed trusted plugin's id. Once loaded, its PLUGIN_INFO/PLUGINS entry silently overwrites the legitimate plugin's entry; subsequent handle_ui_event/handle_server_event/handle_client_event calls addressed to the trusted id are now routed to the attacker's plugin code (spoofing an existing, possibly higher-trust plugin), and management operations (uninstall/reload) that key off id now operate on the attacker's chosen id string, which can itself carry path-traversal or shell-metacharacter payloads feeding the other findings in this slice.
candidate.preconditions: plugin_framework feature; attacker needs their (unsigned) plugin loaded at all.
candidate.confidence_reason: The missing validation is explicit and undisputed in the code and comments; standalone impact (id collision/spoofing) is more modest than the chained path-traversal/injection findings that consume this same unchecked value, hence the lower severity assigned to it on its own.
candidate.disposition_hint: supporting finding — cite as the enabler of the attacker-controlled 'id' feeding the macOS shell-injection and absolute-path findings

verdict.reason: Read the full load_plugin_path (plugins.rs:355-404) plus desc.rs and mod.rs. The claim is accurate on every point: `id = desc.meta().id.clone()` comes straight from the plugin's own `desc()` FFI export, deserialized via `Desc::from_cstr` -> `serde_json::from_str::<Desc>` (desc.rs:80-83) into a plain `id: String` field (desc.rs:57) with zero format/uniqueness checks. The function's own comments at lines 361-362 ('// to-do validate plugin' / '// to-do check the plugin id (make sure it does not use another plugin's id)') confirm the gap is acknowledged-but-unimplemented. `id` is inserted unchecked as the HashMap key into both PLUGIN_INFO (line 370) and PLUGINS (line 400), so a second plugin loaded with a colliding id silently overwrites the first entry — no canonicalize/prefix-check, no signature verify, no permission gate anywhere in this path. I additionally verified the 'used elsewhere as a filesystem path component' side-claim: `get_plugin_dir(id) = get_plugins_dir()?.join(id)` (mod.rs:147-149) does a raw path join with no traversal sanitization, corroborating that this same unchecked id feeds path construction downstream (manager.rs:286, plugins.rs:414). I also traced the remote-reachability angle the finding references: `PluginRequest` messages route via `handle_client_event(&p.id, ...)` on the host (connection.rs:3569-3571) and `handle_server_event` on the controller (io_loop.rs:1989-1990), but those only dispatch to an *already-loaded* plugin keyed by id — they cannot themselves force-load a colliding plugin, so the collision/spoof requires the attacker's plugin to already be loaded locally (feature-gated behind `plugin_framework`, which is not a default Cargo feature per Cargo.toml:33). The candidate is honest about this precondition ('attacker needs their (unsigned) plugin loaded at all') and already self-labels this as a supporting/enabler finding at Medium with 0.55 confidence rather than overclaiming standalone High/Critical impact. I found no mitigating check anywhere in the cited region or its callers that would refute the claim. Severity as submitted (Medium, potential High) is well-calibrated for a keying/collision bug that is real but requires a co-occurring plugin-loading primitive to matter — no correction needed.

candidate.title: Windows: unquoted plugin_id/plugin_url passed as ShellExecuteW lpParameters — argument injection into the elevated re-exec
candidate.root_cause: elevate_install (manager.rs:164-176) / elevate_uninstall (manager.rs:206-208) build a single argument string via format!("--plugin-install {}", plugin_id) / format!("--plugin-install {} {}", plugin_id, plugin_url) with no quoting, then hand it to crate::platform::elevate(&args) -> run_uac(exe, arg) -> ShellExecuteW(..., lpParameters=warg, ...). Because plugin_id/plugin_url are unquoted, any whitespace in them is tokenized by the OS's standard command-line parsing when the elevated child process reads its own argv, letting extra argv entries be smuggled into the Administrator-privileged re-exec.
candidate.entry_point: plugin_id (the plugin's self-declared Meta.id, see companion finding) or plugin_url (built from a remote source's meta.id/version).
candidate.sink: ShellExecuteW(..., lpParameters=warg, ...) in platform/windows.rs run_uac(), invoked from manager.rs elevate() call sites with the unescaped combined string.
candidate.attack: A plugin sets its id to `x --some-other-cli-flag` (any whitespace-separated token core_main.rs recognizes as a privileged action). elevate_uninstall/elevate_install builds `--plugin-install x --some-other-cli-flag` as one string and ShellExecuteW('runas', ...) launches rustdesk.exe elevated with that as its command line; Windows' standard argv tokenization splits it into separate arguments, so the elevated (Administrator) process parses and executes --some-other-cli-flag instead of/in addition to the intended plugin-install action.
candidate.preconditions: Windows build with plugin_framework feature; requires a plugin with a whitespace-containing id to have been loaded, and the user to trigger install/uninstall and approve the UAC prompt; actual impact is bounded by which other CLI switches core_main.rs exposes and whether any of them are independently dangerous when run elevated with attacker-chosen sub-arguments.
candidate.confidence_reason: The unquoted-string-to-ShellExecuteW mechanism is real and verifiable from the code, but ShellExecuteEx does not itself invoke a shell (unlike the macOS `do shell script` sink), so severity depends on enumerating which of rustdesk's many other CLI flags are reachable and dangerous when smuggled in this way — not verified here, hence lower confidence than the macOS variant.
candidate.disposition_hint: needs follow-up — enumerate core_main.rs CLI flags reachable via argument injection and assess which are dangerous when run as Administrator

verdict.reason:
Mechanism is real but the candidate substantially overstates reachability and impact.

CONFIRMED as code fact: manager.rs:170-176 (`elevate_install`) and :206-208 (`elevate_uninstall`) build `format!("--plugin-install {}", plugin_id)` / `format!("--plugin-install {} {}", plugin_id, plugin_url)` with zero quoting (the code even says so at line 169: "to-do: Support args with space in quotes"), and hand it to `platform::elevate()` -> `run_uac(exe, arg)` (windows.rs:2412-2420, :2380-2400) which passes it verbatim as `lpParameters` to `ShellExecuteW(..., "runas", ...)`. Windows tokenizes that string via standard argv rules when the elevated child parses `GetCommandLineW()`, so whitespace in plugin_id/plugin_url does reach the elevated re-exec's argv. That part of the claim stands.

But three things the candidate did not verify sink the claimed severity:

1. Entry point is not reachable as described. `get_plugin_source_list()` (manager.rs:58-66) returns `vec![]` — the remote plugin source is commented out in this build ("Only one source for now"). So the candidate's "plugin_url (built from a remote source's meta.id/version)" vector is dead code here.

2. `install_plugin(id)` (manager.rs:225-226) only proceeds for an `id` that is already a key in `PLUGIN_INFO`, which — given the empty remote source list — is populated exclusively from already-installed local plugins (`load_plugin_list`, manager.rs:140-157). A first-time, never-installed plugin with a crafted whitespace-containing id cannot reach `elevate_install` through this build's UI/IPC flow; the id has to already be on disk as an "installed" plugin, which is itself a chained precondition this finding doesn't establish.

3. The dispatcher doesn't behave like "any CLI switch can be smuggled." core_main.rs:50-81 shows only four literal tokens (`--elevate`, `--run-as-system`, `--quick_support`, `--no-server`) are stripped from the reconstructed argv regardless of position; everything else must exactly fill the `args.len()==2`/`==3` match at core_main.rs:735-747 or the whole `--plugin-install`/`--plugin-uninstall` action silently becomes a no-op — args[0] can never become e.g. `--uninstall-cert` because that literal prefix is fixed by the format string. I traced the one real consequence: smuggling `" --elevate"` into plugin_id causes `core_main.rs:182-185` to fire `elevate_or_run_as_system(false, true, false)` *instead of* the intended install, which (windows.rs:2466-2493, already-elevated branch) calls `run_as_system()` — pivoting the process from Administrator (already user-consented via the same UAC prompt) to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. That's a real but lateral move within a privilege level the attack already required consent for, not a new trust boundary, and it replaces rather than adds to the intended action — the opposite of the candidate's "instead of/in addition to" framing being open-ended.

Net: the unquoted-ShellExecuteW mechanism is a genuine hygiene bug worth fixing (quote/validate), but as scoped its entry point is dead code (empty remote source) or requires an already-planted local plugin (unestablished companion precondition), and the demonstrated consequence is a narrow Admin→SYSTEM lateral pivot rather than arbitrary dangerous-flag injection.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same technical root cause as claimed (unquoted format! string fed to ShellExecuteW lpParameters, tokenized by standard Windows argv parsing in the elevated child), but the practically exploitable consequence is narrower: only 4 literal global flags (--elevate/--run-as-system/--quick_support/--no-server) are extractable from any position in core_main.rs's arg loop; anything else either becomes inert URL text or silently no-ops the whole action because the plugin-install dispatch requires an exact args.len()==2/3 match. The entry point itself (plugin_id/plugin_url) is not reachable through this build's shipped config: get_plugin_source_list() is empty, and install_plugin(id) only accepts ids already present in PLUGIN_INFO, which absent a remote source comes solely from already-installed local plugins.
verdict.live_test: Not required to establish the code-level facts above (Windows ShellExecuteW/CommandLineToArgvW tokenization is documented, standard behavior, and the core_main.rs dispatch logic was read directly). If full end-to-end confirmation is desired: on a Windows build with plugin_framework enabled, manually place a plugin package under the local plugins dir whose Meta.id is `x --elevate`, load it so it appears as "installed" in PLUGIN_INFO, run a portable (not-installed) build, trigger uninstall via the plugin manager UI, approve the UAC prompt, and observe (via Process Monitor / task manager) whether the resulting rustdesk.exe process runs as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM instead of performing the plugin uninstall — this would empirically confirm the one concrete consequence traced above.

candidate.title: Content-Length equality used as a substitute for integrity check lets a local user plant a file that the SYSTEM updater trusts and executes without ever downloading/verifying it
candidate.root_cause: check_update() in updater.rs (lines 160-194) treats "a file of the expected byte length already exists at the predictable download path" as proof the update was already fetched, and skips the download entirely -- it never hashes or otherwise validates the file's contents, only its size (`if file_size == total_size { is_file_exists = true; }`, line 177-178). The path itself (`get_update_download_file_from_url`, line 294-328) is `std::env::temp_dir().join(<predictable filename>)`, a world-writable-for-new-files, per-account shared temp directory. Because this whole check_update() flow only runs inside the main RustDesk service process (gated by `crate::platform::is_installed() && crate::is_server()` in rendezvous_mediator.rs:124-127), that service (and therefore std::env::temp_dir()) resolves to the SYSTEM account's temp directory (C:\Windows\Temp), whose default ACL lets any local standard user CREATE a new file there (just not overwrite one owned by someone else).
candidate.entry_point: A local, unprivileged Windows user account that can create a new file in C:\Windows\Temp before the SYSTEM RustDesk service does. The exact target filename (rustdesk-<version>-<arch>.<ext> or rustdesk-<version>-x86-sciter.exe) and the exact Content-Length of the legitimate release are both learnable from the same public https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest endpoint and the public GitHub release page, so no race/timing skill is required -- the attacker can pre-plant the file any time after each service (re)start, well before the first background check fires (30s delay) or before a manual check.
candidate.sink: src/updater.rs:198-201 -> #[cfg(target_os="windows")] update_new_version(update_msi, &version, &file_path) -> either crate::platform::update_me_msi(p, true) (windows.rs:3649, runs `msiexec /i "<attacker file>"`) or crate::platform::launch_privileged_process(session_id, &format!("{} --update", p)) (updater.rs:251-254 -> windows.rs:807 LaunchProcessWin, which duplicates winlogon.exe's token to launch the process with SYSTEM privileges in the interactive session).
candidate.trace: attacker creates C:\Windows\Temp\rustdesk-<known-version>-<arch>.exe with malicious content padded/crafted to exactly match the real release's Content-Length -> SYSTEM service wakes (30s after start, or every ~10min-1day) -> check_update() (updater.rs:120) sees update available, builds download_url, calls get_download_file_from_url -> file_path.exists()==true (updater.rs:161) -> metadata().len() == HEAD Content-Length (updater.rs:164-178) -> is_file_exists=true, download is skipped entirely -> has_no_active_conns() true -> update_new_version(...) is called on the attacker's file -> attacker code runs as SYSTEM.
candidate.attack: Unprivileged local Windows user (or malware already running at standard-user integrity) queries https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest (or the RustDesk GitHub releases page) to learn the exact expected update filename and its byte size, crafts a malicious PE/MSI of identical length, writes it to C:\Windows\Temp\<expected-filename> as soon as the RustDesk service starts (well before the size-based short-circuit fires), and waits for the next auto-update cycle (or triggers one, since a version bump is required upstream but auto-update intervals are as short as 10 minutes on retry). Result: the malicious file is installed/launched by the SYSTEM-privileged RustDesk service -> local privilege escalation to SYSTEM.
candidate.preconditions: Windows only. Requires: (1) RustDesk installed as a service (`is_installed() && is_server()`), which is the default install mode; (2) a genuine newer version currently available upstream (drives SOFTWARE_UPDATE_URL non-empty) OR the attacker simply waits for/knows the next real release version in advance; (3) attacker has any local standard-user account able to create new files in C:\Windows\Temp (default Windows ACL permits this); (4) `has_no_active_conns()` true at trigger time (no active remote sessions -- trivially satisfiable by an idle machine, which is exactly when auto-update fires).
candidate.confidence_reason: The logic is directly readable in updater.rs: size-only equality gates a full download skip, the path is temp_dir()-based and predictable, and the SYSTEM-service execution context is corroborated by rendezvous_mediator.rs's is_installed()/is_server() gate and windows.rs's LaunchProcessWin/winlogon-token mechanism. Residual uncertainty: exact default ACL of C:\Windows\Temp can vary by Windows build/hardening policy, and I have not dynamically verified on a live host that a standard user can win file-creation there ahead of the SYSTEM service (would need live confirmation).
candidate.disposition_hint: high-value candidate for live Windows validation: confirm default C:\Windows\Temp ACL allows unprivileged file creation, then reproduce end-to-end (plant same-length file, trigger manual check, observe SYSTEM process spawned from the planted file).

verdict.reason: Direct code-read confirms the core mechanism exactly as claimed: (1) updater.rs:294-328 get_update_download_file_from_url() builds a predictable path std::env::temp_dir().join(<version+arch filename>) after strict github.com URL validation; (2) updater.rs:160-182 uses ONLY a size comparison (local metadata().len() == remote Content-Length from an HTTP HEAD) as the sole 'already downloaded' check -- no hash/signature is ever computed, confirmed by grep finding zero signature/hash/checksum references anywhere in updater.rs or windows.rs; (3) on a size match the download is skipped and the pre-existing file_path is fed straight to update_new_version() -> either `msiexec /i "<file>"` (windows.rs:3649-3654, update_me_msi) or launch_privileged_process() (windows.rs:807-826), which calls the native LaunchProcessWin API to duplicate winlogon.exe's token and run the file in the interactive session with elevated/SYSTEM rights -- no Authenticode/signature check in either path; (4) this whole flow is confirmed reachable only from the RustDesk process gated by `crate::platform::is_installed() && crate::is_server()` in rendezvous_mediator.rs:125-126, i.e. the SYSTEM service, so std::env::temp_dir() does resolve to the SYSTEM-account temp dir (C:\Windows\Temp by default, no TEMP/TMP env override found anywhere in the codebase). All of that is exactly as the candidate describes. HOWEVER, I found a materially incomplete precondition: check_update() (updater.rs:123-125) first requires `manually || config::Config::get_bool_option(OPTION_ALLOW_AUTO_UPDATE)`, and `option2bool()` (config.rs:2829-2841) treats any key prefixed `allow-` as defaulting to OFF (value must literally be "Y"; empty/unset -> false) with DEFAULT_SETTINGS starting empty -- so 'Auto update' (flutter/lib/desktop/pages/desktop_setting_page.dart:554-559, config key allow-auto-update, isServer:true, shown only when Windows+installed) is an admin-facing checkbox that is UNCHECKED by default. Worse, the `manually=true` branch the candidate's timeline implicitly relies on ('before a manual check') is dead code in this checkout: `manually_check_update()` (updater.rs:37-41) is `#[allow(dead_code)]` and I grepped the entire repo (src/, flutter/, libs/) -- nothing calls it; the flutter 'Check for software update on startup' checkbox (kOptionEnableCheckUpdate) wires to a completely different function, `check_software_update()`/`do_check_software_update()` in common.rs, which only populates SOFTWARE_UPDATE_URL and never touches updater.rs's download/skip/install logic at all. So on a stock RustDesk install, check_update()'s vulnerable body (lines 126-201) NEVER executes -- the only entry into it is the always-manually=false background thread, itself gated by an opt-in, admin-only, off-by-default setting. This is a real, code-verified precondition the candidate omitted, not a guessed/assumed mitigation, so it changes the likelihood characterization materially: this is not something any idle default RustDesk install exposes -- it requires the machine's admin to have already turned on 'Auto update'. Once that non-default condition is met, the rest of the chain (predictable path, size-only 'integrity' bypass, zero signature check, SYSTEM execution via msiexec/duplicated winlogon token) is fully confirmed and severe.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same mechanical root cause as claimed (size-equality used as a download-skip heuristic on a predictable, low-priv-writable temp path, with no hash/signature check before SYSTEM-privileged execution via msiexec or a duplicated winlogon token) -- but gated behind config key allow-auto-update (updater.rs:123), an admin-only, Windows+installed-only UI checkbox (desktop_setting_page.dart:554-559) that defaults to OFF (option2bool 'allow-' prefix semantics, config.rs:2829-2841). The candidate's alternate 'manual check' trigger does not exist as a reachable path: manually_check_update() (updater.rs:37) has zero callers anywhere in the repo and is marked dead_code, so there is no way to force check_update(true) short of the missing/nonexistent caller. Preconditions list should read: local unprivileged Windows account able to create a new file in C:\Windows\Temp (needs live ACL confirmation) AND the machine's RustDesk install already has the non-default 'Auto update' setting enabled by an admin AND a genuinely newer upstream release exists.
verdict.live_test: On a disposable Windows VM: (1) install RustDesk as a service, enable the 'Auto update' checkbox in Settings, confirm allow-auto-update=Y is persisted in the machine-wide Config store; (2) as a low-privileged standard-user account (no admin), attempt `echo test > C:\Windows\Temp\rustdesk-test-<n>.tmp` to confirm default ACL permits file creation by non-owners; (3) query https://api.rustdesk.com/version/latest (or GitHub releases) for the current release's exact filename+Content-Length, craft a same-length payload PE/MSI, write it to C:\Windows\Temp\<expected filename> as the standard user; (4) either wait for the next background check_update() tick or, since manually_check_update() is unreachable, restart the RustDesk service to hit the 30s startup check; (5) observe via Process Monitor/Task Manager whether msiexec or the planted file is launched from a SYSTEM-token process, confirming size-only bypass and unsigned SYSTEM execution end-to-end.
verdict.observed_mitigation: updater.rs:123-125 gates the entire download/exists-check/install flow behind config::Config::get_bool_option(OPTION_ALLOW_AUTO_UPDATE); option2bool() (libs/hbb_common/src/config.rs:2829-2841) makes any 'allow-' prefixed key default to false/OFF when unset, and DEFAULT_SETTINGS starts empty, so this is off by default. The alternate manually=true trigger (manually_check_update(), updater.rs:37) has no callers anywhere in the repository (confirmed by full-repo grep), so it is not a reachable alternate path in this build.

candidate.title: Downloaded update artifact is never hash- or signature-verified before being installed/executed with SYSTEM privileges
candidate.root_cause: check_update() (updater.rs:120-204) downloads the update binary over HTTPS and writes the raw response bytes straight to disk (`std::fs::File::create(&file_path)?; file.write_all(&file_data)?;`, lines 192-193) with no accompanying integrity control: no published checksum/hash is fetched or compared, and no code-signature (Authenticode) verification is performed anywhere in the Rust code before update_new_version() (windows.rs) either runs `msiexec /i "<file>"` (windows.rs:3649-3654, update_me_msi) or directly executes the downloaded EXE with SYSTEM privileges via launch_privileged_process (updater.rs:251-254). The only defense is that the download URL is domain/path-locked to github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/releases/download/... (get_update_download_file_from_url, updater.rs:294-329) and fetched via a TLS-cert-validating client (create_http_client_with_url_strict, hbbs_http/http_client.rs:142-166, danger_accept_invalid_cert=false) -- i.e. authenticity relies entirely on the TLS chain to github.com and the integrity of GitHub's release pipeline / api.rustdesk.com's response, with zero independent signature check as a defense-in-depth layer.

candidate.title: Unquoted file path in the privileged process command line built for the downloaded update executable

If the SYSTEM account's temp directory path ever contains a space (e.g., a non-default %TEMP%/%SystemRoot% configuration), Win32 CreateProcess's unquoted-command-line parsing tries several path prefixes split at each space before the space-delimited executable name, which is the classic "unquoted path" hijack primitive.

candidate.confidence_reason: The missing quoting is directly visible in the source and is inconsistent with the quoted form used in run_exe_in_session elsewhere in the codebase, but default Windows temp paths have no spaces, so real-world exploitability depends on a non-default environment I cannot confirm from source alone.

I confirmed the inconsistency the candidate cites: `run_exe_in_session` (windows.rs:872, `format!("\"{}\" {}", exe, ...)`) and `launch_server` (windows.rs:800-801, `format!("\"{}\" --server", ...)`) both quote; `update_new_version`'s exe-update branch does not. candidate.component: Terminal service session registry (server::terminal_service reconnect path, gated from server::connection terminal login)

All cited line numbers check out.

However, tracing where terminal.service_id actually comes from refutes the practical exploitability the candidate builds on. client.rs:2753 shows the CONTROLLER populates LoginRequest.Terminal.service_id from its own LOCAL config option (client.rs:2829-2835: key "terminal-service-id"/"terminal-admin-service-id"), which is only ever written back into that same local config after a successful TerminalOpened response on the SAME connection (io_loop.rs:2120-2123: `lc.set_option(key, opened.service_id.clone())`). flutter.rs:1133-1137 pushes `opened.service_id` only into the originating connection's own event stream — never to any other controller. terminal_service::list_services() (terminal_service.rs:216-224), the only function that could enumerate other sessions' service_ids, is defined but is not called or exposed via any RPC/IPC anywhere in src/ (grep confirms zero callers). Default IDs are server-generated via `format!("ts_{}", uuid::Uuid::new_v4())` (terminal_service.rs:105-107, invoked at connection.rs:5738-5740) — 122 bits, brute force infeasible. So the "attacker knows/predicts/leaked the victim's service_id" precondition the candidate flags as unverified is, on this codebase's actual data flow, unsupported: there is no discovered channel by which controller B ever learns controller A's service_id. A client CAN self-fixate its own service_id (server accepts a non-empty client-supplied value verbatim on first login, connection.rs:5738 `if self.terminal_service_id.is_empty()`), but that only lets an attacker collide with themselves, not force a victim onto a chosen ID absent an out-of-band collusion/shared-config scenario the candidate does not demonstrate.

Rating this High/Critical overstates real-world risk; it belongs as a hardening recommendation pending discovery of an actual service_id leak channel (e.g., via CM/admin UI, logs exposed to other principals, or a future API), which was not found here.

verdict.reason:
Re-derived the entire chain from source and every step in the candidate's trace matches the code exactly.

1. terminal_service.rs:162-199 `get_or_create_service()`: uses `HashMap::entry().or_insert_with()` to get-or-create by `service_id`, then UNCONDITIONALLY calls `service.lock().unwrap().reset_status(is_persistent)` at line 196 — this executes on the pre-existing-service path too, not just on creation.
2. `reset_status()` (949-956): overwrites `self.is_persistent = is_persistent` (the CALLER's value, not the original owner's) and force-sets `session.state = SessionState::Closed` for every session in the service, unconditionally.
3. `terminal_service::new()` (388-405), called from `connection.rs:5741` `init_terminal_service()`, passes the CURRENT connection's own `is_persistent`/`user_token` straight into `get_or_create_service()` with zero binding check against who created the existing entry.
4. `run()` (407-429): when the GenericService loop exits (i.e., when the calling connection's service instance is torn down / connection disconnects), it checks `!service.lock().unwrap().is_persistent` and calls `remove_service(&service_id)` if true.
5. `remove_service()` (201-213) locks and calls `session.stop()` on every session still registered — including sessions belonging to a DIFFERENT (victim) connection that happened to share the `service_id`.
6. `TerminalSession::stop()` (779-873) confirmed to end with `if let Some(mut child) = self.child.take() { let _ = child.kill(); ... }` — a real process kill, not just a flag flip.

PersistentTerminalService (884-892) has no owner/creator binding field at all — only `service_id`, `sessions`, timestamps, `is_persistent`, `is_specified_user`. `is_specified_user` is set once at creation via the `or_insert_with` closure and never re-validated against a would-be reconnector's identity for an EXISTING entry.

I specifically hunted for a mitigating ownership check and found the closest candidate: `connection.rs:3880-3899` in `prepare_terminal_login_for_authorization()`, which compares `terminal_service::is_service_specified_user(service_id)` against the connecting client's own `has_service_token`. I verified this does NOT block the attack: on Linux/macOS, `TerminalUserToken::to_terminal_service_token()` (connection.rs:295-301) only has the `SelfUser` variant, which always maps to `None` — so both `is_user` (recorded at service creation) and `has_service_token` (computed for the new connecting client) are always `false`, making the mismatch check `false != false` → always pass, a no-op for the default terminal-login mode. Even on Windows, the check only compares the *class* of token (OS-login vs not) — it never compares connection/session identity — so two different attacker-controlled connections both using the same login class (the common case) sail through this check identically to how the legitimate owner would.
